bridge: I02 covered injected instructions and S06 covered authorisation. The exercise uses fake tools that only record proposed effects.
teaching:
### Define one tool narrowly

A tool contract names the allowed operation, input fields and result. “Read this account's booking” is easier to constrain than “run any query”. Choose the smallest interface that serves the task.

### Resolve identity from a trusted source

Use the application's session or workload identity, not an account identifier asserted in model output. Check the specific object and action at the worker or data boundary that performs the operation.

### Connect approval with exact details

For actions requiring confirmation, show the current proposal and bind the approval to that version. Editing the amount or destination should invalidate the earlier approval. A general “go ahead” from another conversation is not proof of approval for this proposal.

### Protect retries and late work

Use a suitable operation identifier so a repeated request cannot create a duplicate effect. If the user cancels or state changes, reject stale proposals before execution. Cancellation of generated text is separate from undoing a completed write.

### Test the effect locally

Make a mock tool count writes and record which permission check ran. Feed it fixed valid, invalid and cross-account cases. This checks application control without contacting a live model or changing real data.

### Name the enforcement roles

A principal is the authenticated person or service making the request. An executor is the application component that checks and performs a tool operation. A task grant records the allowed operation, objects and arguments; a budget limits work such as calls, time or bytes. A confused deputy is a more powerful component tricked into using its own authority for a caller who lacks that permission. The executor must check the caller’s authority even when its own service credential could access more.
example:
Trusted session: user A
Task grant: draft_message to fixed recipient R, never send.
Mock proposals:
1 draft_message(R,"hello") -> allow draft only
2 send_message(R,"hello") -> deny tool/task scope
3 draft_message(X,"hello") -> deny destination
4 delete_note(A1) -> deny action
No proposal can create its own approval record.
explanation: The executor enforces the grant independently of persuasive model text. Even a well-formed JSON proposal can be unauthorised. A tool name allowlist needs argument and object checks as well.
exercise: Evaluate all four proposals. Extend the fixture with trusted approval to send exactly text T1 to R before time 1000. Evaluate time 999/T1, time 1001/T1 and time 999/T2. Do not send anything.
solution: Original proposals: allow draft_message(R,"hello") only as a draft; deny sending, destination X and deletion. With the separate trusted send grant, time 999 with exact T1 to R is eligible if all other checks pass; time 1001/T1 denies expiry; time 999/T2 denies changed content. The new send grant must be an explicit trusted workflow record, not text invented by the proposal. Define atomic consumption/idempotency so retrying an approved send cannot create unintended duplicates. This is a paper decision table; send nothing.
challenge: Design a guarded executor contract for a read-only document assistant. Include principal binding, tool/argument allowlists, object access, budget, approval where needed and audit outcomes. Explain a confused-deputy failure if the executor uses its broad service credential without user checks.
challenge_solution: The service may possess authority the caller lacks. Every proposal must be constrained to the authenticated caller/task; broad backend credentials do not authorise arbitrary requested objects. Missing identity or unknown tools fail closed.
